4.54321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.50945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.86389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\}\mathtt{a}\mathtt{b}\mathtt{c}\mathtt{a}\{\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-8.18211pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{\mathsf{x}_{3}}}}_{{\kern-7.68211pt{}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.50945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.86389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-8.18211pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{\mathsf{x}_{3}}}}_{{\kern-7.68211pt{}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.50945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.86389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-5.74321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.6321pt{\mathsf{x}_{3}}}}_{{\kern-5.24321pt{}\kern 5.6321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.50945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.86389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-4.65433pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 4.54321pt{\mathsf{x}_{3}}}}_{{\kern-4.15433pt{}\kern 4.54321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.17778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.50945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.86389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\}
). However, the definition with repeated occurrences of
\Gamma_{i}
will be more convenient for proving the results of this section. Later on, in Section
6.2
, we shall also use this simplified version of the marker-set representation.

The next propositions point out the relevant properties of the marker-set representation. The first one is a direct consequence of the definition of the marker-set representation, the second one follows from the first one. We state these propositions mainly for demonstrating the meaning of the marker-set representation and for general illustrational purposes; for our results, the ref-word analogues of Proposition
5
and
6
(formally stated as Lemmas
10
and
11
) are more important and shall be proven in detail.

Proposition 5
.

Let
w_{1},w_{2}
be subword-marked words. Then
\mathfrak{e}(w_{1})=\mathfrak{e}(w_{2})
and
\mathsf{st}(w_{1})=\mathsf{st}(w_{2})
if and only if
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
.

Proposition 6
.

Let
L_{1},L_{2}
be subword-marked languages. Then
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
if and only if
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
.

Note that the above proposition states that
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
is characteristic for the inclusion of the corresponding spanners (i. e.,
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
), but not for the inclusion of the corresponding subword-marked languages
L_{1}
and
L_{2}
. More precisely,
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
is not a sufficient condition for
L_{1}\subseteq L_{2}
(although, as can be easily seen, it is a necessary condition).

5.1.
Model Checking and Non-Emptiness

We now consider the problem
\mathsf{ModelChecking}
(recall that this is the problem to decide whether
t\in S(w)
for given spanner
S
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
,
w\in\Sigma^{*}
and
(\mathcal{X},w)
-tuple
t
).

Theorem 7
.

\mathsf{ModelChecking}
for
\reflspanners
can be solved in time
\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|M|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
, where
M
is an
\NFA
that represents a refl-spanner
S=\left\llbracket\lang(M)\right\rrbracket
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
,
w\in\Sigma^{*}
, and
t
is an
(\mathcal{X},w)
-tuple.

Proof 5.1
.

For convenience, we will assume that every symbol in
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
occurs in some transition of
M
(this is w.l.o.g., because if
\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-10.44156pt{\mathsf{x}}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-15.41232pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-10.44156pt{\mathsf{x}}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-15.41232pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-7.3571pt{\mathsf{x}}\kern 5.6321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-10.90765pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.6321pt{}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-6.26822pt{\mathsf{x}}\kern 4.54321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-9.81877pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 4.54321pt{}}}}
or
\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-8.18211pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\kern-7.68211pt{}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-8.18211pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\kern-7.68211pt{}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-5.74321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.6321pt{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\kern-5.24321pt{}\kern 5.6321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-4.65433pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 4.54321pt{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\kern-4.15433pt{}\kern 4.54321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
does not, we can safely remove
\mathsf{x}
from
\mathcal{X}
and reject
t
in case that
\mathsf{x}\in\textup{dom}(t)
). In particular,
|\mathcal{X}|\leqslant|M|
.

The proof is split in two parts. First, we consider the
regular case
, where
\lang(M)
is not a ref-language, but just a subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
(i. e.,
\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket
is a regular spanner). The algorithm for this case is then used for the general
refl case
where
\lang(M)
is a ref-language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
(i. e.,
\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket
is a refl-spanner).

Regular case:
We shall denote by
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
the
\NFA

M
with the modification that we interpret each transition labelled with some
\sigma\in\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
as a transition that can read any symbol
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
with
\sigma\in\Gamma
. This means that
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
accepts a language over the alphabet
\Sigma\cup\mathcal{P}({\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}})
and, moreover, for every
w\in\lang(M)
and arbitrary subword-marked word
w^{\prime}
with
\mathsf{msrep}(w)=\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
(this includes
w
itself), we have that
w^{\prime}\in\lang(\mathsf{msrep}(M))
.

By definition,
t\in\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket(w)
if and only if there exists a subword-marked word
v\in\lang(M)
such that
\mathsf{st}(v)=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v)=w
. This latter property can be checked as follows.

We first combine
t
and
w
into a subword-marked word
w^{\prime}
, i. e.,
\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(w^{\prime})=w
(the order in which we place consecutive occurrences of symbols from
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
is not relevant). In the following, we shall consider
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
(the construction of which we discuss later on), and the automaton
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
as explained above.

{clm}

The following statements are equivalent:

(1) There exists a subword-marked word
v\in\lang(M)
such that
\mathsf{st}(v)=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v)=w
.

(2)
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})\in\lang(\mathsf{msrep}(M))
.

Proof 5.2
.

We start with “(1)
\implies
(2)” and assume that there exists a subword-marked word
v\in\lang(M)
such that
\mathsf{st}(v)=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v)=w
. The fact
\mathfrak{e}(v)=w
means that
v
equals
w
with some (possibly empty) factors over
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
between the symbols of
\Sigma
. Moreover,
\mathsf{st}(v)=t
means that if in
v
we replace each maximal factor
\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\ldots\sigma_{k}
over
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
with
\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{k}\}^{k}
, we get exactly
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, and, by construction of
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
, the fact that
v\in\lang(M)
also implies that
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})\in\lang(\mathsf{msrep}(M))
(i. e.,
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
accepts
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
via the same sequence of states).

Next, we prove “(2)
\implies
(1)” and assume that
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})\in\lang(\mathsf{msrep}(M))
, which means that there is an accepting run of
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
on
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
. By construction, each transition of this run that reads a symbol
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
is a re-interpretation of an original
\sigma
-transition of
M
for some
\sigma\in\Gamma
. Consequently, for every symbol
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, there is a well-defined
representative

\sigma\in\Gamma
. If we replace every symbol
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
in
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
by its representative, then we obtain a
word
v
over
\Sigma\cup\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
, and by construction of

\mathsf{msrep}(M)
, we also have
v\in\lang(M)
, which means that
v
is a
subword-marked word. By construction of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, it is also
obvious that
\mathfrak{e}(v)=\mathfrak{e}(\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime}))=w
. Moreover, in
the construction of
v
, every factor in
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
of the form

\Gamma^{|\Gamma|}
with
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
, is replaced by
a factor
\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\ldots\sigma_{|\Gamma|}
with
\sigma_{i}\in\Gamma
for every
i\in[|\Gamma|]
. Since
v
is a
subword-marked word, this means that
\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{|\Gamma|}\}=\Gamma
, which means that
(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{|\Gamma|})
is some linear ordering of
\Gamma
. By
construction of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, this directly implies that

\mathsf{st}(v)=t
.

Claim
5.1
means that in order to check whether
t\in\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket(w)
, it is sufficient to check whether
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})\in\lang(\mathsf{msrep}(M))
. Therefore, we shall now discuss how we can efficiently check
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})\in\lang(\mathsf{msrep}(M))
. First, we have to construct (a suitable representation of)
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, which we do in the following way.

Let us assume that
w^{\prime}=\gamma_{1}w_{1}\gamma_{2}w_{2}\ldots\gamma_{n}w_{n}\gamma_{n+1}
, where
w=w_{1}w_{2}\ldots w_{n}
and the
\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots,\gamma_{n+1}
are (possibly empty) factors over
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
. Consequently,

\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})=(\Gamma_{1})^{|\Gamma_{1}|}w_{1}(\Gamma_{2})^{|\Gamma_{2}|}w_{2}\ldots(\Gamma_{n})^{|\Gamma_{n}|}w_{n}(\Gamma_{n+1})^{|\Gamma_{n+1}|}

according to the definition of
\mathsf{msrep}(\cdot)
. Let us further assume that we have some fixed order on
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
.
We initialise an array
A
of size
n+1
in time
O(n)
. Then we move over
w^{\prime}
from left to right, and whenever we encounter some
\gamma_{i}=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\ldots\sigma_{n_{i}}
, we construct a binary search tree (with respect to the order on
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
) of the elements of
\Gamma_{i}=\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{n_{i}}\}
, and we store this search tree in entry
i
of
A
. For this, we have to consider each symbol from
w^{\prime}
only once and we have to insert at most
|\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}|
symbols from
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
into a binary search tree of size at most
|\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}|
. Consequently, this can be done in time
\bigO(|w^{\prime}|+(|\mathcal{X}|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))=\bigO(|w|+(|\mathcal{X}|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
. We then represent
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
as the
string
1^{|\Gamma_{1}|}w_{1}2^{|\Gamma_{2}|}w_{2}\ldots n^{|\Gamma_{n}|}w_{n}(n+1)^{|\Gamma_{n+1}|}
and the array
A
, where the symbols
i

point to the
i^{\text{th}}
entry of
A
.

With this representation of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, we can read
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
with
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
, and every transition can be evaluated in constant time for symbols from
\Sigma
, and in time
\bigO(\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
for symbols from
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
. More precisely, transitions labelled with symbols from
\Sigma
can be evaluated in constant time by directly comparing the next input symbol with the transition label from
\Sigma
, while for evaluating transition labels from
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
, we have to check whether the input symbol
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
(from
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
) contains the transition label, which, since we have
\Gamma
represented as binary search tree, can be done in time
\bigO(\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
. Consequently, we can check whether
\mathsf{msrep}(M)
accepts
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
in time
\bigO(|\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})|\cdot|\mathsf{msrep}(M)|\cdot\log(|\mathcal{X}|))=\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|M|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
. Since this also dominates the time needed for constructing the representation of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, the total running time is
\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|M|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
.

Refl case:
In this case,
t\in\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket(w)
if and only if there is some
v\in\lang(M)
such that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=w
. We next show how this latter property can be checked.

For every
\mathsf{x}\in\textup{dom}(t)
let
w_{\mathsf{x}}
be the subword of
w
that corresponds to
t(\mathsf{x})
, i.e.,
w_{\mathsf{x}}=w[i,j\rangle
if
[i,j\rangle=t(\mathsf{x})
. Next, we obtain an
\NFA

M^{\prime}
from
M
by replacing every
\mathsf{x}
-transition for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
by a path of transitions labelled with the word
w_{\mathsf{x}}
. It is important to observe that
M^{\prime}
accepts a subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
(indeed, replacing the references of ref-words by some factors over
\Sigma
necessarily yields valid subword-marked words).

{clm}

The following statements are equivalent:

(1) There exists a ref-word
v\in\lang(M)
such that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=w
.

(2) There exists a subword-marked word
v^{\prime}\in\lang(M^{\prime})
such that
\mathsf{st}(v^{\prime})=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v^{\prime})=w
.

Proof 5.3
.

We start with “(1)
\implies
(2)” and assume that there exists some
v\in\lang(M)
such that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=w
. Since
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=t
, we know that
\mathfrak{d}(v)
equals the word obtained from
v
by replacing each occurrence of a reference
\mathsf{x}
by the word
w_{\mathsf{x}}
. Hence, defining
v^{\prime}:=\mathfrak{d}(v)
, we have
v^{\prime}\in\lang(M^{\prime})
, and, by assumption,
\mathsf{st}(v^{\prime})=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v^{\prime})=w
.

Next, we prove “(2)
\implies
(1)” and assume that there exists some
v^{\prime}\in\lang(M^{\prime})
such that
\mathsf{st}(v^{\prime})=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v^{\prime})=w
. We obtain a word
v
from the accepting run of
M^{\prime}
on
v^{\prime}
as follows. We simply trace all the symbols in the order read by the transitions, but whenever we read some
w_{\mathsf{x}}
by some of the paths that
M
’s
\mathsf{x}
-transitions have been replaced with, we use the symbol
\mathsf{x}
instead of the factor
w_{\mathsf{x}}
.
By construction of
M^{\prime}
, we have
v\in\lang(M)
, which means that
v
is a ref-word and therefore
\mathfrak{d}(v)
is well-defined. Furthermore, since
\mathsf{st}(v^{\prime})=t
and by construction of the
w_{\mathsf{x}}
, we also have
\mathfrak{d}(v)=v^{\prime}
. Finally, by assumption, we have
\mathsf{st}(v^{\prime})=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v^{\prime})=w
, which implies
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=w
.

We observe that Claim
5.1
means that in
order to check
t\in\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket(w)
, it is
sufficient to check whether there exists a subword-marked word
v\in\lang(M^{\prime})
(recall that
M^{\prime}
accepts a subword-marked language) such that
\mathsf{st}(v)=t
and
\mathfrak{e}(v)=w
. This latter task is exactly the
regular case
discussed above; thus, it can be done in time
\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|M^{\prime}|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
.
However, since we obtained
M^{\prime}
from
M
by replacing some transitions by paths of
\bigO(|w|)
transitions, we can only bound
|M^{\prime}|=\bigO(|w|\cdot|M|)
. This yields an overall upper bound of
\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|w|\cdot|M|\cdot\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
, which is quadratic in
|w|
. We shall now discuss how we can use a standard data-structure for strings in order to implement our algorithmic idea more efficiently.

Let us recall that the algorithm for the refl case first constructs
M^{\prime}
by replacing
\mathsf{x}
-transitions by
w_{\mathsf{x}}
-paths, then we re-interpret the
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
-transitions of
M^{\prime}
as described in the
regular case
, and then we check whether this
\NFA
accepts
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
(for a suitable
w^{\prime}
obtained from
w
and
t
). The whole improvement consists in just keeping the
\mathsf{x}
-transitions instead of replacing them by
w_{\mathsf{x}}
-paths, but then, when checking whether
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
is accepted, we nevertheless want to treat
\mathsf{x}
-transitions as
w_{\mathsf{x}}
-transitions, but in constant time (i. e., we want to check whether the remaining input starts with
w_{\mathsf{x}}
in constant time), for which we need the data structure. More precisely, we will compute a data structure that allows us to check, for every position
i
of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
and every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, whether
w_{\mathsf{x}}
is a prefix of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})[i..|\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})|]
in constant time.
With this addition to the algorithm, the overall running time is still
\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|M^{\prime}|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))

(note that for this it is vital that we can check
in constant time
whether the remaining input starts with
w_{\mathsf{x}}
), but we have
|M^{\prime}|=\bigO(|M|)
, which leads to the overall running time
\bigO((|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)|M|\log(|\mathcal{X}|))
. Let us now give the details for the improvement.

For a word
u
and for every
i\in[|w|{+}1]
let
\textsf{suff}_{i}(u)
be the suffix of
u
starting at position
i
of
u
. A
longest common extension
data structure
\lce_{u}
for a word
u
is defined such that
\lce_{u}(i,j)
, for
i,j
with
1\leqslant i<j\leqslant|u|
, is the length of the longest common prefix of
\textsf{suff}_{i}(u)
and
\textsf{suff}_{j}(u)
. It is known that (see, e. g.,
[
FH06
]
)
\lce_{u}
can be constructed in time
\bigO(|u|)
and afterwards
\lce_{u}(i,j)
can be retrieved in constant time for arbitrary given
i
and
j
.

We construct
\lce_{w\hat{w}}
, where
\hat{w}
is obtained from

\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
by replacing all symbols from
\mathcal{P}({\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}})
by a
new symbol
\#
, i. e.,
\#\notin\Sigma\cup\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
(note
that
|\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})|=|\hat{w}|
and these words only differ with
respect to symbols
\mathcal{P}({\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}})
and
\#
). Now, for a given

\mathsf{x}\in{\mathcal{X}}
with
t(\mathsf{x})=[i_{\mathsf{x}},j_{\mathsf{x}}\rangle
, and position
i
of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, we
have that
w_{\mathsf{x}}
is a prefix of
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})[i..|\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})|]
if
and only if
\lce_{w\hat{w}}(i_{\mathsf{x}},|w|+i)\geqslant j_{\mathsf{x}}-i_{\mathsf{x}}
. Finally, observe that
\lce_{w\hat{w}}
can be
constructed in time
\bigO(|w\hat{w}|)=\bigO(|w|+|\mathcal{X}|)
.
This completes the proof of Theorem
7
.

We discuss a few particularities about Theorem
7
. The result points out that
\mathsf{ModelChecking}
for refl-spanners has the same complexity as for regular spanners,
4
4

4

To the best knowledge of the authors, the bound that is provided by Theorem
7
is also the currently best upper bound for model checking of regular spanners in the literature.
which can be considered surprising, given the fact that refl-spanners cover a large class of core spanners and are generally much more expressive than regular spanners. Moreover, for core spanners the problem
\mathsf{ModelChecking}
is
\npclass
-complete. Another interesting fact is that in data complexity,
\mathsf{ModelChecking}
can be solved in linear time for both regular as well as refl-spanners (whereas the latter result is slightly more complicated, since it depends on using the longest common extension data structure).

Next, we consider the problem
\NonemptProb
(i. e., to decide whether
S(w)\neq\emptyset
for given
S
and
w
), for which we can obtain the following theorem by standard methods.

Theorem 8
.

\NonemptProb
for
\reflspanners
is
\npclass
-complete.

Proof 5.4
.

The
\npclass
-hardness can be proven in a similar way as Theorem 3.3 in
[
FH18
]
. It follows easily by a reduction from the problem of matching patterns with variables, which is as follows: for a given pattern
\alpha\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal{X})^{*}
and a word
w\in\Sigma^{*}
, decide whether there is a mapping
h\colon\mathcal{X}\to\Sigma^{*}
such that
\widehat{h}(\alpha)=w
, where
\widehat{h}
is the natural extension of
h
to a morphism
(\mathcal{X}\cup\Sigma)^{*}\to(\mathcal{X}\cup\Sigma)^{*}
, by letting
h
be the identity on
\Sigma
. This problem is
\npclass
-complete (for more information see, e. g.,
[
FSV16
,
FS15
,
FH18
]
).

Let
\alpha\in(\mathcal{X}\cup\Sigma)^{*}
be a pattern with variables and let
w\in\Sigma^{*}
. Moreover, let
\beta
be the regular expression obtained from
\alpha
by replacing each first occurrence of a variable
\mathsf{x}
by
\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-10.44156pt{\mathsf{x}}\kern . It can be easily seen that
\lang(\beta)
is a ref-language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, and that
w\in\lang(\alpha)
if and only if

. This shows that
\NonemptProb
for
\reflspanners
is

-hard.

For membership in
\npclass
, let
S=\left\llbracket\lang(M)\right\rrbracket\in\reflspanners_{\Sigma,\mathcal{X}}
and let
w\in\Sigma^{*}
. In order to check whether
S(w)\neq\emptyset
, we guess some
(\mathcal{X},w)
-tuple
t
, which can be done in polynomial time. Then we check whether
t\in S(w)
, which can also be done in polynomial time (see Theorem
7
).

5.2.
Static Analysis

We start with the following straightforward result. Recall that for the problems
\SatProb
,
\HierProb
and
\FunctProb
, we get a single spanner
S
, represented by an
\NFA
, as input and ask whether there is a
w\in\Sigma^{*}
with
S(w)\neq\emptyset
, whether
S
is hierarchical, or whether
S
is functional, respectively.

Theorem 9
.

(1)

\SatProb
for
\reflspanners
can be solved in time
\bigO(|M|)
,

(2)

\HierProb
for
\reflspanners
can be solved in time
\bigO(|M|\cdot|\mathcal{X}|^{3})
, and

(3)

\FunctProb
for
\reflspanners
can be solved in time
\bigO(|M|\cdot|\mathcal{X}|^{2})
,

where
M
is an
\NFA
that describes a refl-spanner over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
.

Proof 5.5
.

1
: Let
S\in\reflspanners_{\Sigma,\mathcal{X}}
be represented by an
\NFA

M
.

If
\lang(M)\neq\emptyset
, then there is a
v\in\lang(M)
and therefore, by definition,
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))\in\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket(\mathfrak{e}(v))
, which means that
S(\mathfrak{e}(v))\neq\emptyset
.
On the other hand, if there is some
w\in\Sigma^{*}
with
S(w)\neq\emptyset
, then there is a span-tuple
t\in\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket(w)
, which means that there is a ref-word
v\in\lang(M)
with
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=w
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v))=t
. Thus,
\lang(M)\neq\emptyset
. Consequently, there is a word
w\in\Sigma^{*}
with
S(w)\neq\emptyset
if and only if
\lang(M)\neq\emptyset
. Checking whether
\lang(M)\neq\emptyset
can be done in time
\bigO(|M|)
, by searching
M
for a path from the start state to an accepting state.

2
:
Let
S\in\reflspanners_{\Sigma,\mathcal{X}}
be represented by an
\NFA

M
. It is straightforward to see that
S
is hierarchical if and only if
\lang(M)
is hierarchical. According to Proposition
3
the latter can be checked in time
\bigO(|M|\cdot|\mathcal{X}|^{3})
.

3
:
Let
S\in\reflspanners_{\Sigma,\mathcal{X}}
be represented by an
\NFA

M
. It is straightforward to see that
S
is functional if and only if
\lang(M)
is functional. According to Proposition
3
the latter can be checked in time
\bigO(|M|\cdot|\mathcal{X}|^{2})
.

With respect to Theorem
9
, it is worth recalling that for core spanners,
\SatProb
and
\HierProb
are
\pspaceclass
-complete, even for restricted classes of core spanners (see
[
FH18
]
).

Finally, we investigate the problems
\ContProb
and
\EquProb
, which consist in deciding whether
S_{1}\subseteq S_{2}
or
S_{1}=S_{2}
, respectively, for given spanners
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
.

Recall that for core spanners
\ContProb
and
\EquProb
are not semi-decidable (see
[
FH18
]
). We now show that for refl-spanners we can achieve decidability of
\ContProb
and
\EquProb
by imposing suitable restrictions.

Let us first briefly discuss the case of regular spanners. Let
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
be regular spanners represented by
\NFA
s
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
. Due to Proposition
6
, we can check whether
S_{1}\subseteq S_{2}
by checking whether
\mathsf{msrep}(\lang(M_{1}))\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(\lang(M_{2}))
. Checking whether
\mathsf{msrep}(\lang(M_{1}))\not\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(\lang(M_{2}))
can be done in
\pspaceclass
(i. e., we guess a witness
w^{\prime}
and check whether
w^{\prime}\in\mathsf{msrep}(\lang(M_{1}))\setminus\mathsf{msrep}(\lang(M_{2}))
); we skip all the details here, since the result will follow from our more general result with respect to a subclass of refl-spanners; moreover, the
\pspaceclass
-completeness of containment of regular spanners has already been mentioned in
[
MRV18
]
.

Let us give some intuition of why the situation is more complicated for refl-spanners. We first note that also for ref-words (since they are subword-marked words), we can use the function
\mathsf{msrep}(\cdot)
. However, while
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
for ref-words
w_{1},w_{2}
is still sufficient for
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
, it is not a necessary condition. For example, the ref-words

\mathcal{X}_{e,\mathsf{x}}

\mathsf{x}
.

Lemma 10
.

Let
w_{1}
and
w_{2}
be strongly reference extracting ref-words over
\Sigma
and
(\mathcal{X}_{r},\mathcal{X}_{e},\{\mathcal{X}_{e,\mathsf{x}}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{r}\})
. Then
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
if and only if
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
.

Proof 5.6
.

If
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
, then we obviously also have
\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
. Since both
\mathfrak{d}(w_{1})
and
\mathfrak{d}(w_{2})
are subword-marked words, we can use Proposition
5
to conclude that
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))
.

Next, we assume that
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
. Since both
\mathfrak{d}(w_{1})
and
\mathfrak{d}(w_{2})
are subword-marked words, we can conclude with Proposition
5
that
\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
. In order to conclude the proof, we have to show that
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
. To this end, we show that the assumption
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})\neq\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
leads to a contradiction.

We prove by induction that, for every
i\in\{0,1,\ldots,\max\{|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})|,|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})|\}\}
,
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[1,i+1\rangle=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[1,i+1\rangle
. As the base of the induction, we observe that
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[1,0+1\rangle=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[1,1\rangle=\varepsilon
and
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[1,0+1\rangle=\varepsilon
. Next, we assume that, for some
i\in\{0,1,\ldots,\max\{|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})|,|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})|\}-1\}
, we have that
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[1,i+1\rangle=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[1,i+1\rangle
. We let

\sigma_{1}=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[i+1,i+2\rangle
and
\sigma_{2}=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[i+1,i+2\rangle
. We make a case distinction with respect to
\sigma_{1}
(note that by symmetry this will cover all possible cases).

Case
\sigma_{1}\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
: In this case,
\sigma_{1}\neq\sigma_{2}
would directly imply that for some
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, we have that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))(\mathsf{x})\neq\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))(\mathsf{x})
(note that this holds for all possible choices of
\sigma_{2}
). Hence, we would get the contradiction that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))\neq\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
, which implies that we have
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}
.

Case
\sigma_{1}\in\Sigma
and
\sigma_{2}\in\Sigma
: This directly implies that there is some position
j
such that
\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))[j,j+1\rangle=\sigma_{1}
and
\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))[j,j+1\rangle=\sigma_{2}
. Thus, since
\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))=\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
, we can directly conclude that
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}
.

Case
\sigma_{1}=\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{r}
: If
\sigma_{2}\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
, then we can proceed like in the first case, but with
\sigma_{2}
playing the role of
\sigma_{1}
. Hence, we may assume that
\sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{X}\cup\Sigma
. By Point
1
of Observation
5.2
, we can conclude that
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[i,i+1\rangle=\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
such that
\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-10.44156pt{\mathsf{y}}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-15.41232pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-10.44156pt{\mathsf{y}}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-15.41232pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-7.3571pt{\mathsf{y}}\kern 5.6321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-10.90765pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.6321pt{}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-6.26822pt{\mathsf{y}}\kern 4.54321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-9.81877pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 4.54321pt{}}}}\in\Gamma
for some
\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{X}_{e,\mathsf{x}}
. By assumption, we therefore also have
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[i,i+1\rangle=\Gamma
. Hence, Point
2
of Observation
5.2
implies that symbol
\Gamma
at position
i
of
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
is followed by a sequence of occurrences of
\Gamma
followed by
\mathsf{x}
. Since we made the assumption that
\sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{X}\cup\Sigma
, we know that
\sigma_{2}\neq\Gamma
, which means that
\sigma_{2}=\mathsf{x}
. Consequently,
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}
.

We have shown that

\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})[1,i+1\rangle=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[1,i+1\rangle
holds
for every
i\in\{0,1,\ldots,\max\{|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})|,|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})|\}\}
. This means that either
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
, or one of these words is a proper prefix of the
other. Let us assume that the latter case applies and, without loss of
generality, that
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})
is a proper prefix of

\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
. More formally, for some
j\in\{|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})|,|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})|+1,\ldots,|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})|\}
, we have that

\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[1,j+1\rangle=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})
, and
|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})|>|\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})|
. If
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[j+1,j+2\rangle\in\Sigma
or

\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[j+1,j+2\rangle\in\mathcal{X}
, then
|\mathfrak{d}(w_{2})|>|\mathfrak{d}(w_{1})|
, which leads to the contradiction that

\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))\neq\mathsf{msrep}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
(note that in the
latter case, i. e.,
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[j+1,j+2\rangle\in\mathcal{X}
, it is
important that for strongly reference extracting ref-words we require
for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{r}
with
|w|_{\mathsf{x}}\neq 0
that

\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w))(\mathsf{x})=[i,j\rangle
with
j-i\geqslant 2
). Moreover, if
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})[j+1,j+2\rangle=\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
, then, for some
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, we have that

\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))(\mathsf{x})\neq\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))(\mathsf{x})
. This leads to the contradiction
that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{1}))\neq\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w_{2}))
. Consequently, it is not possible that one
of
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})
or
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
is a proper prefix of the other;
thus,
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
.
This concludes the proof of Lemma
10
.

Lemma 11
.

Let
L_{1},L_{2}
be strongly reference extracting ref-languages over
\Sigma
and
(\mathcal{X}_{r},\mathcal{X}_{e},\allowbreak\{\mathcal{X}_{e,\mathsf{x}}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{r}\})
. Then
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
if and only if
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
.

Proof 5.7
.

Let us first assume that
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
. Let
v_{1}\in\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})
and let
v^{\prime}_{1}\in L_{1}
be such that
\mathsf{msrep}(v^{\prime}_{1})=v_{1}
. Moreover, let
w=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{1}))
, which also means that
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{1}))\in\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket(w)
. Since
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
, we have
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket(w)\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket(w)
and therefore
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{1}))\in\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket(w)
. By definition, this means that there is some
v^{\prime}_{2}\in L_{2}
with
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{2}))=w=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{1}))
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{2}))=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v^{\prime}_{1}))
. By Proposition
10
, this means that
\mathsf{msrep}(v^{\prime}_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(v^{\prime}_{2})
, and, by definition,
\mathsf{msrep}(v^{\prime}_{2})\in\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
. Thus,
\mathsf{msrep}(v^{\prime}_{1})=v_{1}\in\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
. Since
v_{1}\in\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})
has been chosen arbitrarily, we can conclude that
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
.

Next, we assume that
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
. Let
w\in\Sigma^{*}
and
t\in\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket(w)
be arbitrarily
chosen. This means that there is some
v_{1}\in L_{1}
with

\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v_{1}))=w
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v_{1}))=t
. By
assumption,
\mathsf{msrep}(v_{1})\in\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
, which means that there is some
v_{2}\in L_{2}
with
\mathsf{msrep}(v_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(v_{2})
, which, by Proposition
10
, means that
\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v_{1}))=\mathfrak{e}(\mathfrak{d}(v_{2}))=w
and
\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v_{1}))=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(v_{2}))=t
. Thus,
t\in\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket(w)
. Since
w\in\Sigma^{*}
and
t\in\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket(w)
have been chosen arbitrarily, we can conclude that
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
.

Theorem 12
.

\ContProb
and
\EquProb
for strongly reference extracting refl-spanners over
\Sigma
and
(\mathcal{X}_{r},\mathcal{X}_{e},\{\mathcal{X}_{e,\mathsf{x}}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{r}\})
are
\pspaceclass
-complete.

Proof 5.8
.

We first note that hardness follows from the fact that the inclusion and equivalence problem for
\NFA
s is
\pspaceclass
-hard (see
[
MS72
,
SM73
]
). Next, we prove the upper bound for the case of
\ContProb
(which also implies the upper bound for
\EquProb
). Note that the general proof idea is very similar to
[
MRV17
, Thm. 6.4]
, i. e., the
\pspaceclass
-completeness of regular spanners with schemaless semantics.

Let
L_{1},L_{2}
be strongly reference extracting ref-languages over

\Sigma
and
(\mathcal{X}_{r},\mathcal{X}_{e},\{\mathcal{X}_{e,\mathsf{x}}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{r}\})
, represented by
\NFA

M_{1}
and
M_{2}
. We
wish to decide whether
\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket L_{2}\rrbracket
. By Lemma
11
, this
can be done by checking whether
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
. We shall now devise a nondeterministic algorithm that
checks whether
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\not\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
. Note that we cannot modify automata for
L_{1}
and
L_{2}
in polynomial space such that they accept the languages
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})
and
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
, respectively.

Without loss of generality, we assume that
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
are complete. The algorithm guesses words
w_{1},w_{2}
over
\Sigma\cup\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}\cup\mathcal{X}
letter by letter, which satisfy
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
, and checks whether
w_{1}
is accepted by
M_{1}
and rejected by
M_{2}
. To this end, we run the automata in parallel and, since the automata are nondeterministic, we have to explore all possible paths labelled with
w_{1}
and
w_{2}
, which can be done by maintaining the sets
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
of current active states of
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
, respectively. More precisely, we guess the next symbols
\sigma_{1}
and
\sigma_{2}
of
w_{1}
and
w_{2}
, and then we update the sets of active states by applying the
\sigma_{1}
- and
\sigma_{2}
-transitions for the active states of
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
, respectively. Obviously, in order to satisfy
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
, we must have
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}
whenever
\sigma_{1}\in\Sigma\cup\mathcal{X}
. If, however, in
w_{1}
we guess that instead of a symbol from
\Sigma
or
\mathcal{X}
a sequence over
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
follows, then we must process with
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
all possible permutations of this sequence. This can be done as follows. If we guess the next
\sigma_{1}
to be neither from
\Sigma
or from
\mathcal{X}
, we guess a set
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
instead. Then we enumerate all linear orders
\vec{\Gamma}
of the symbols from
\Gamma
, and for each such
\vec{\Gamma}
, we update the sets of active states by exploring all
\vec{\Gamma}
-labelled paths in
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
that start in states of
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
, respectively. Moreover, after such a step, the algorithm must next again guess some
\sigma_{1}
from
\Sigma
or
\mathcal{X}
.

We start this procedure with
S_{1}=\{s_{0,1}\}
and
S_{2}=\{s_{0,2}\}
, where
s_{0,1}
and
s_{0,2}
are the initial states of
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
, respectively. The algorithm terminates with output
\mathsf{yes}
as soon as
S_{1}
contains an accepting state and
S_{2}
does not contain an accepting state. Note that if
S_{1}
contains an accepting state, then this also means that the currently read input
w_{1}
is a valid ref-word, which, since
\mathsf{msrep}(w_{1})=\mathsf{msrep}(w_{2})
, also means that
w_{2}
is a valid ref-word.

We shall now consider the correctness of the algorithm. The basic observation is that, for some (nondeterministically chosen) word over
w\in\Sigma\cup\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}\cup\mathcal{X}
, the algorithm simulates
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
in parallel on
all
inputs
w^{\prime}
that satisfy
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})=\mathsf{msrep}(w)
.
If
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\not\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
, then there is some
w\in\lang(M_{1})
such that for every
w^{\prime}
over
\Sigma\cup\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}\cup\mathcal{X}
with
\mathsf{msrep}(w)=\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, we have that
w^{\prime}\notin\lang(M_{2})
. Consequently, if the algorithm guesses
w
(this means it guesses
w
’s symbols from
\Sigma\cup\mathcal{X}
in the right order, and whenever some sequence
\gamma
over
\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
follows, it guesses the set
\Gamma
that contains exactly the symbols from
\gamma
), then, after having completely read
w
, we will reach a set of active states
S_{1}
with an accepting state, while, due to
w^{\prime}\notin\lang(M_{2})
for all
w^{\prime}
with
\mathsf{msrep}(w)=\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})
, the set
S_{2}
of active states cannot contain an accepting state. This means that the algorithm produces output
\mathsf{yes}
. On the other hand, if the algorithm produces output
\mathsf{yes}
, then it has guessed some
w
such that, once it its completely consumed,
S_{1}
contains an accepting state while
S_{2}
does not contain any accepting state. Consequently,
\lang(M_{1})
accepts some
w^{\prime}
with
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime})=\mathsf{msrep}(w)
, while there is no
w^{\prime\prime}\in\lang(M_{2})
with
\mathsf{msrep}(w^{\prime\prime})=\mathsf{msrep}(w)
. This directly implies that
\mathsf{msrep}(w)\in\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})
and
\mathsf{msrep}(w)\notin\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
; thus,
\mathsf{msrep}(L_{1})\not\subseteq\mathsf{msrep}(L_{2})
.

With respect to the complexity of the algorithm, we observe that we only store sets
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
that are subsets of the states of
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
, respectively. Furthermore, updating these steps can be easily done in polynomial space by consulting the transition functions of
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
. In particular, we observe that guessing a set
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
and enumerating all linear orders
\vec{\Gamma}
of the symbols from
\Gamma
can also be done in polynomial space.

6.
Expressive Power of Refl-Spanners

It is a straightfoward observation that the expressive power of refl-spanners properly exceeds the one of regular spanners, but it is less clear which refl-spanners are also core spanners and which core spanners are refl-spanners.

6.1.
From Refl-Spanners to Core Spanners

A ref-language
L
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
is
reference-bounded
if there is a number
k
with
|w|_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant k
for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
and every
w\in L
. A refl-spanner is
reference-bounded
if it is represented by a reference-bounded ref-language. The following is easy to see.

Theorem 13
.

Every reference-bounded refl-spanner is a core spanner.

Proof 6.1
.

Let
S
be a refl-spanner over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
represented by an
\NFA

M
, and let
k\in\mathbb{N}
be such that
|w|_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant k
for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
and every
w\in\lang(M)
. For every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, let
\mathcal{Y}_{\mathsf{x}}=\{\mathsf{y}_{\mathsf{x},1},\mathsf{y}_{\mathsf{x},2},\ldots,\mathsf{y}_{\mathsf{x},k}\}
be
k
fresh variables. We define an
\NFA

M^{\prime}
as follows. The automaton
M^{\prime}
simulates
M
, but for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, it maintains a counter
c_{\mathsf{x}}
in its finite state control that is initially
0
and that can hold values from
\{0\}\cup[k]
. Whenever
M
takes an
\mathsf{x}
-transition,
M^{\prime}
increments
c_{\mathsf{x}}
and then can read any word from
\lang(\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{y}_{\mathsf{x},c_{\mathsf{x}}}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[11.58273pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[11.58273pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[8.97408pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[8.32852pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-17.15619pt{\mathsf{y}_{\mathsf{x},c_{\mathsf{x}}}}\kern . It can be easily seen that
\lang(M^{\prime})
is a subword-marked language over

and
\mathcal{X}
. Furthermore, it can be shown with moderate effort that
\llbracket\lang(M)\rrbracket=\pi_{\mathcal{X}}\varsigma^{=}_{\{\mathcal{Y}_{\mathsf{x}}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}}(\llbracket\lang(M^{\prime})\rrbracket)
.

It is interesting to note that the refl-spanner

, which is
not
reference-bounded, is provably not a core spanner (see
[
FKRV15
, Theorem 6.1]
)).

6.2.
From Core Spanners to Refl-Spanners

The question of which core spanners can be represented as refl-spanners is a much more difficult one and we shall investigate it in more detail. There are simple core spanners which translate to refl-spanners in an obvious way, e. g.,

. For an in-depth analysis of the capability of core spanners to describe word-combinatorial properties, we refer to

.

These considerations suggest that the refl-spanner formalism is less powerful than core spanners, which is to be expected, since we have to pay a price for the fact that we can solve many problems for refl-spanners much more efficiently than for core spanners (see our results presented in Section
5
and summarised in Table
1
). However, we can show that a surprisingly large class of core spanners can nevertheless be represented by a single refl-spanner along with the application of a simple spanner operation (to be defined in the next subsection) that just combines several variables (or columns in the spanner result) into one variable (or column) in a natural way, and a projection; see Theorem
19
for our respective main result.

We again extend the function
\mathsf{msrep}(\cdot)
in the natural way to a subword-marked language
L
by setting
\mathsf{msrep}(L)=\{\mathsf{msrep}(w)\mid w\in L\}
.

Remark 14
.

In this section, we assume that all our regular and refl-spanners are represented as (automata that accept) subword-marked languages and ref-languages, respectively, all the words of which are given in marker-set representation. It can be easily seen that any
\NFA
accepting a subword-marked language or a ref-language can be transformed into an
\NFA
that accepts the
\mathsf{msrep}(\cdot)
image of that language. This transformation may cause an exponential blow-up, which is no problem, since we are here only concerned with questions of expressive power, and not with complexity issues.

We next give an intuitive explanation of the result to be proven in
this subsection. As the central question of this subsection, we
investigate which core spanners of the form
S=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
(where
L
is a regular
subword-marked language) can be described by
\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket
for some regular ref-language
L^{\prime}
. Our first respective
observation is that
S
can in fact be described in the form

\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket
for a regular ref-language
L^{\prime}
, provided
that all the variables that are subject to the string-equality
selection
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
are
simple
(with respect to

L
). A variable
\mathsf{x}
is called simple with respect to a subword-marked language
L
, if any definition for
\mathsf{x}
(in any
w\in L
) is always of the form
\Gamma_{1}u\Gamma_{2}
with
\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
,
\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathsf{x}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleright^{{\kern-10.44156pt{\mathsf{x}}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\kern-15.41232pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern Next, we show that we can use this result in order to prove that a much larger class of
core spanners can also be described by ref-languages, if we also allow
an additional operation on spanners, which we call the

span-fusion

\bigspanfusion
. Intuitively, for a set
\lambda=\{\mathsf{y}_{1},\mathsf{y}_{2},\ldots,\mathsf{y}_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{X}
of
variables, and a completely new variable
\mathsf{x}
with
\mathsf{x}\notin\mathcal{X}
, the span-fusion
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}

replaces in a span-relation the set of columns
\{\mathsf{y}_{1},\mathsf{y}_{2},\ldots,\mathsf{y}_{k}\}
by a single new column
\mathsf{x}
that, for each
row
t
(i. e., span-tuple
t
), contains a single span that
corresponds to the union of all the spans
t(\mathsf{y}_{1}),t(\mathsf{y}_{2}),\ldots,t(\mathsf{y}_{k})
. For example,
\bigspanfusion_{\{\mathsf{x}_{1},\mathsf{x}_{2}\}\to\mathsf{z}}
turns a
\{\mathsf{x}_{1},\mathsf{x}_{2},\mathsf{x}_{3}\}
-tuple
t=([3,17\rangle,[17,23\rangle,[4,20\rangle)

into a
\{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{x}_{3}\}
-tuple
t^{\prime}
with
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{z})=[3,23\rangle
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}_{3})=[4,20\rangle)
. The span-fusion operation will be formally defined below in Section
6.2.2
.

We can show that provided that
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
satisfies a certain

non-overlapping
property (basically, we require that any two
variables that are subject to the string-equality selection are
non-overlapping with respect to
L
), we can represent

\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
in the form
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda_{1}\to\mathsf{x}_{1}}\bigspanfusion_{\lambda_{2}\to\mathsf{x}_{2}}\ldots\bigspanfusion_{\lambda_{k}\to\mathsf{x}_{k}}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)
for a regular ref-language
L^{\prime}
over
\Sigma
and a set
\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
of variables with
|\mathcal{X}^{\prime}|=\bigO(|\mathcal{X}|^{3})
.

The proof idea for this result is as follows (formal details are given later on). Every regular
subword-marked language
L
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
can be
transformed into a subword-marked language
L^{\prime}
over
\Sigma
and

\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
such that, for every
w\in L
, there is a
w^{\prime}\in L^{\prime}
with

\mathfrak{e}(w)=\mathfrak{e}(w^{\prime})
and
\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})
is a
split

of
\mathsf{st}(w)
. An
\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
-tuple
t^{\prime}
is a split of an

\mathcal{X}
-tuple
t
, if every span
t(\mathsf{x})=[\ell_{\mathsf{x}},r_{\mathsf{x}}\rangle
is factorised into
\varno
factors
with respect to
t^{\prime}
, i. e., there are variables
\mathsf{x}^{1},\mathsf{x}^{2},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{\varno}\in\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
such that
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})=[\ell_{\mathsf{x}},k_{1}\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{2})=[k_{1},k_{2}\rangle,\ldots,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{\varno-1})=[k_{\varno-1},k_{\varno}\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{\varno})=[k_{\varno},r_{\mathsf{x}}\rangle
(the number

\varno
is explained later and satisfies
\varno=\bigO(|\mathcal{X}|^{2})
). Moreover, we require these factorisations to be
such that the spans for any two variables are non-overlapping. The
subword-marked language
L^{\prime}
of all these splits of subword-marked
words from
L
will be called the
split
of
L
, and it can be
shown that if
L
is regular, then so is its split
L^{\prime}
. In
particular, by definition of the span-fusion, we immediately have that

\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\llbracket L\rrbracket
, where
\Lambda=\{\lambda_{\mathsf{x}}\to\mathsf{x}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}
with
\lambda_{\mathsf{x}}=\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\mathsf{x}^{2},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{\varno}\}
for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
. The split-operation will be formally defined below in Section
6.2.3
.

The next idea is that we can simulate the string-equality selection

\varsigma_{E}^{=}
(for
L
) with
E=\{\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}\}
directly on the split

L^{\prime}
. Intuitively speaking, for every
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
, we require the pairs
\mathsf{x}^{j},\mathsf{y}^{j}
to be
subject to a string-equality selection for every
j\in[\varno]
, or,
more formally, we define the string-equality selection

\varsigma^{=}_{E^{\prime}}
, where
E^{\prime}=\{\mathcal{Y}_{i}^{j}\mid i\in[k],j\in[\varno]\}
and
\mathcal{Y}_{i}^{j}=\{\mathsf{x}^{j}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}\}
for
i\in[k]
and
j\in[\varno]
. It can be
easily seen that if
t\in\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)(w)
for some
w\in\Sigma^{*}
, then we also have
t\in\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)(w)
. The converse, however, is only true if
t
has a
split
t^{\prime}
that is in
\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)(w)
. A split
t^{\prime}
of
t
is only in

\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)(w)
if, for every
i\in[k]
, all
t(\mathsf{x})
with
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
are factorised
into the parts
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1}),t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{2}),\ldots,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{\varno})
in exactly the same way, since otherwise
t^{\prime}

would not satisfy
\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}
. In the general case, the set

\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
of variables is not large enough to make such a split
t^{\prime}

possible for every
t\in\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)(w)
. The problem is that due to the property of
t^{\prime}
that
all the spans for each two variables of
\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
are
non-overlapping, the number of variables needed for this property may
depend on
|w|
(as will also be demonstrated below by an
example). This, however, can only happen if
E
is
overlapping
,
i. e., there are variables
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\bigcup_{i\in[k]}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
such that the spans of
\mathsf{x}
and
\mathsf{y}
may refer
to overlapping spans. Consequently, we have
\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
, if
E
is
non-overlapping
(see Lemmas
17
and
18
).

Finally, since the split
L^{\prime}
of
L
has necessarily only simple variables, we can express
\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)
as
\llbracket L^{\prime\prime}\rrbracket
for a regular ref-language
L^{\prime\prime}
(recall that this was our first result, sketched at the beginning of this subsection). Consequently,
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
can be expressed as
\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\llbracket L^{\prime\prime}\rrbracket)
, where
L^{\prime\prime}
is a regular ref-language.

In the following subsections, we shall formally carry out this proof roadmap.

6.2.1.
Simple Variables

As sketched above, a variable is called simple with respect to a
subword-marked language if all its definitions do not contain parts of
other variable definitions, i. e., symbols
\Gamma\subseteq\mathcal{X}
. We will show next that string-equality selections for simple variables can be expressed by the ref-language mechanism, i. e., by using variable references.

Our next goal is to show that for a subword-marked language
L
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, and an
E=\{\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
such that all variables from
\bigcup_{i\in[k]}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
are simple with respect to
L
, we can construct a regular ref-language
L^{\prime}
such that
\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\varsigma_{\mathcal{Z}}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
; see Theorem
15
below. We first sketch the intuitive idea of the construction and then give a formal proof.

for at least one
\mathsf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}
. The first step is to remove all subword-marked words that have both non-empty and empty
\mathcal{Z}
-definitions, since they describe span-tuples that are filtered out by the string-equality selection
\varsigma_{\mathcal{Z}}^{=}
. Moreover, this can be easily done by simply storing in the finite state control whether the first
\mathcal{Z}
-definition is empty or not, and then abort any computation that reads both types of
\mathcal{Z}
-definition.

The next task is to handle all other subword-marked words, i. e.,
those
w\in L
in which some
\mathcal{Z}
-definitions assign to
variables from
\mathcal{Z}
spans referring to different non-empty
strings (which we somehow have to get rid of, since they represent
span-tuples filtered out by the string-equality selection), and those
that assign the same non-empty string to all variables from

\mathcal{Z}
. These properties cannot be explicitly checked by a
finite automaton. The idea of the construction is based on the
observation that for all subword-marked words
w\in L
that assign to
every variable from
\mathcal{Z}
spans referring to the same string,
we can as well only keep the very first
\mathcal{Z}
-definition

\Gamma_{1}u\Gamma_{2}
of
w
, and replace every further
\mathcal{Z}
-definition
\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}u\Gamma^{\prime}_{2}
in
w
by
\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}\widehat{\mathsf{z}}\Gamma^{\prime}_{2}
, where

\widehat{\mathsf{z}}
is some arbitrarily chosen variable defined by the
first
\mathcal{Z}
-definition. Such a modified
w^{\prime}
satisfies
w=\mathfrak{d}(w^{\prime})
and therefore also
\mathsf{st}(w)=\mathsf{st}(\mathfrak{d}(w^{\prime}))
. Consequently, this modification yields a
ref-language
L^{\prime}
with
\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\varsigma_{\mathcal{Z}}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
. Obviously, we
have to show that
L^{\prime}
is regular. To this end, we can directly modify
the
\NFA

M
for
L
as follows. We simulate
M
up to the point
where we read the first
\mathcal{Z}
-definition
\Gamma_{1}u\Gamma_{2}
. However, before reading
u
, we guess a state for every
variable from
\mathcal{Z}
that might be defined by a later

\mathcal{Z}
-definition. Then, while reading
u
, we compute some
states that are reachable from the guessed states by reading
u

(since
M
is nondeterministic, these target states are also
implicitly guessed by the specific path that is chosen). The idea is
of course that if the currently read input turns out to be of the kind
that is not filtered out by
\varsigma_{\mathcal{Z}}^{=}
, then it
must also be possible to guess exactly the state pairs between which
all the further occurrences of
u
are read in the following

\mathcal{Z}
-definitions of
w
(after all, these state pairs must be
such that
u
can be read between them, so it is possible to guess
them while processing the string
u
of the first

\mathcal{Z}
-definition). Then, in the rest of the computation,
whenever we encounter a
\mathcal{Z}
-definition
\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}u^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}_{2}
, we simply verify if we have guessed valid state pairs
(i. e., whether the computation of
M
also ends up in the states
guessed for the variables of this
\mathcal{Z}
-definition when we
encounter this
\mathcal{Z}
-definition), and then we simply read

\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}\widehat{\mathsf{z}}\Gamma^{\prime}_{2}
instead of
\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}u^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}_{2}
. Let us now give a formal proof.

Theorem 15
.

Let
L
be a regular subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, let
E=\{\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
be such that all variables from
\bigcup_{i\in[k]}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
are simple with respect to
L
. There is a regular ref-language
L^{\prime}
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
with
\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
. Furthermore,
L^{\prime}
is reference-bounded.

(the state reached from
s
by reading
u
) and the additionally stored pairs
(s_{\mathsf{z},\openmark},s_{\mathsf{z},\closemark})
are such that, for every
\mathsf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}\setminus\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}_{i}
, reading
u
can change
M
from state
s_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
to
s_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}
(unless
s_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}=\undefin
). In particular, note that the start states
s_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
are non-deterministically guessed, while the states
s_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}
(unless we have
s_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}=\undefin
) are also non-deterministically determined, since there might be several states rechable from
s_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
by reading
u
.

Whenever we encounter a non-empty
\mathcal{Z}_{i}
-definition
\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}u^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}_{2}
, for some
i\in[k]
, that is
not
a first
\mathcal{Z}_{i}
-definition, then we proceed as follows. We let again
\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}^{\prime}_{i}
be the variables from
\mathcal{Z}
defined by this definition. By the way we have processed the first
\mathcal{Z}_{i}
-definition
\Gamma_{1}u\Gamma_{2}
, we know that for every
\mathsf{z}^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}^{\prime}_{i}
, the pair
(s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\openmark},s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\closemark})
is such that we can reach
s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\closemark}
from
s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\openmark}
by reading
u
(or
s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\closemark}=\undefin
). Moreover, recall that
\widehat{\mathsf{z}}_{i}
is an arbitrary variable defined by this first
\mathcal{Z}_{i}
-definition
\Gamma_{1}u\Gamma_{2}
.
Let
s^{\prime}
be the state reached by
M
after having read
\Gamma^{\prime}_{1}
.
We check whether
s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\openmark}=s^{\prime}
for every
\mathsf{z}^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}^{\prime}_{i}
, and whether
s_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime},\closemark}=t^{\prime}
for every
\mathsf{z}^{\prime}\in\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}^{\prime}_{i}
and the same state
t^{\prime}
, and, if this is the case, we read the variable reference
\widehat{\mathsf{z}}_{i}
and move to state
t^{\prime}
.

This concludes the definition of
\mu(M)
. We will show next the correctness of the construction, i. e.,
\lang(\mu(M))=\mu(L_{1})
.

Let
w
be accepted by
M
and assume that
\mu(w)\neq\bot
, i. e.,
\mu(w)\in\mu(L_{1})
. If, for every
i\in[k]
,
w
has at most one non-empty
\mathcal{Z}_{i}
-definition, then
\mu(M)
accepts
\mu(w)=w
(by the same run as
M
accepts
w
). So let us assume that
i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{p}\in[k]
are such that
w
has at least two non-empty
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definitions for
j\in[p]
. Since
\mu(w)\neq\bot
, we know that, for every
j\in[p]
, all
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definitions of
w
define the same factor
u_{j}
, i. e., every non-empty
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition has the form
\Gamma_{1}u_{j}\Gamma_{2}
. We have to show that
\mu(M)
accepts
\mu(w)
.

We assume that, for every
j\in[p]
,
\Gamma^{j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{j}_{2}
is the first
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition of
w
, and let
\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}_{i_{j}}
be the variables from
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
defined by this
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition
\Gamma^{j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{j}_{2}
.
For every
\mathsf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}\setminus\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}_{i_{j}}
that is defined by some

\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition in
w
, let
\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
and
\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}
be the states
between which
M
reads the factor
u_{j}
in the

\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition for
\mathsf{z}
. The
\NFA

\mu(M)
can
now simulate
M
until it encounters the first

\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition
\Gamma^{j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{j}_{2}
. Then,
after reading
\Gamma_{1}^{j}
,
\mu(M)
can guess for every
\mathsf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}\setminus\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}_{i_{j}}
the states
\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
and store them in the components
s_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
, if
w
contains some
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition
that defines

, and it can guess some arbitrary state
otherwise. Then, it can read
u_{j}
in such a way that exactly the

\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}
are stored in the
components
s_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}
, if
w
contains some

\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition that defines
z
, and

\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}=\undefin
otherwise. This must
be possible by definition of these states
\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\openmark}
and
\widetilde{s}_{\mathsf{z},\closemark}
, and by

\mu(M)
’s definition. The
\NFA

\mu(M)
can now proceed with

M
, but whenever it encounters another

\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition
\Gamma^{\prime j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{\prime j}_{2}
, due to
the stored states, it will read
\Gamma^{\prime j}_{1}\widehat{\mathsf{z}}_{j}\Gamma^{\prime j}_{2}
instead of
\Gamma^{\prime j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{\prime j}_{2}
(recall that
\widehat{\mathsf{z}}_{i}
is the fixed variable from
\widehat{\mathcal{Z}}_{i_{j}}
selected earlier). Hence, it accepts the word
\mu(w)
.

On the other hand, let some

be accepted by
\mu(M)
. If, for every
i\in[k]
,
w^{\prime}
has at most one non-empty
\mathcal{Z}_{i}
-definition, then

accepts
w^{\prime}
, and
\mu(w^{\prime})=w^{\prime}
, i. e.,
w^{\prime}\in\mu(L_{1})
. So let us assume that

are such that

has at least two non-empty
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definitions for
j\in[p]
. For every
j\in[p]
, the first
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition has the form
\Gamma^{j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{j}_{2}
, and all other
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definitions have the form
\Gamma^{\prime j}_{1}\widehat{\mathsf{z}}_{j}\Gamma^{\prime j}_{2}
, where

is from the set

of those variables from
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
that are defined by the first
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition
\Gamma^{j}_{1}u_{j}\Gamma^{j}_{2}
.
Moreover, for every such
\mathcal{Z}_{i_{j}}
-definition
\Gamma^{\prime j}_{1}\widehat{\mathsf{z}}_{j}\Gamma^{\prime j}_{2}
where

is read by going from some state

to some state

can read

by going from state

to

(this follows from the definition

). This directly implies that the word

obtained from

by replacing each

satisfies

and

. Thus,

.

We conclude that we have shown that
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket)
, that

\llbracket\mu(L_{1})\rrbracket=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket)
, and that
\mu(L_{1})
is a regular ref-language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
. Thus,
L^{\prime}:=\mu(L_{1})
is a regular ref-language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
with
\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
. Moreover,
L^{\prime}
is obviously reference-bounded.

with

, and

-definitions that are both

-definitions.

For the following, it is a crucial observation that, for every

, the tuple described by

is filtered out by
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
if and only if it is filtered out by
\varsigma_{E_{\sim_{w}}}^{=}
, i. e.,
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\{\mathsf{st}(w)\})=\varsigma_{E_{\sim_{w}}}^{=}(\{\mathsf{st}(w)\})
. Indeed, if the tuple described by

is filtered out by
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
, then it must be filtered out by
\varsigma_{E_{\sim_{w}}}^{=}
as well, since

is a refinement of

. On the other hand, if the tuple described by

satisfies
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
, then, by definition of
\sim_{w}
, it must also satisfy all the string-equality selections described by
E_{\sim_{w}}
.

For every

, we have defined above the condition for

, and we have defined the ref-word

. For every fixed

, these definitions depend only on

. However, we had to require that these sets satisfied our two conditions: (1)

for every

with

, and (2), for every

and for every non-empty

-definition

and every empty

\Gamma_{1}
in

, there is some

such that

, and the ref-word

It is not hard to see that for this adapted version of

, we also have that
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket)
. Indeed, every word

that, for some

-definition and an empty
\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{i}
-definition must be filtered out by
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
.

Moreover, the adapted version of
\mu
also satisfies that, if
w\in L_{1}
with
\mu(w)\neq\bot
, then
\mu(w)
is a ref-word with
w=\mathfrak{d}(\mu(w))
. In particular, this also means that
\llbracket\mu(L_{1})\rrbracket=\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L_{1}\rrbracket)
.

Consequently, also in the general case, we have that
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)=\llbracket\mu(L_{1})\rrbracket
. However, it remains to show that with the adapted definitions of
L_{1}
and
\mu(w)
,
L_{1}
and
\mu(L_{1})
are still regular. In the constructions of the
\NFA
s for
L_{1}
and
\mu(L_{1})
, we have explained how the computation should proceed on a fixed input
w
, and in dependency of the sets
\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}
. Consequently, for a fixed input
w
, we can carry out the constructions also for the sets
\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{1},\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{k_{\sim_{w}}}
, as long as the automaton has knowledge of these sets, which, after all, depend on the input. Hence, we let the
\NFA
s simply initially guess the equivalence relation
\sim_{w}
, and then we will verify this guess while processing the input
w
, and we will abort the computation if the guess of
\sim_{w}
has been incorrect. In this way, we can assume that for any input
w
the sets
\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{1},\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{k_{\sim_{w}}}
are known to the
\NFA
, which means that we can carry out the
\NFA
constructions described above, just with respect to the sets
\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{1},\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}^{\sim_{w}}_{k_{\sim_{w}}}
instead of the set
\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}
.

This completes the proof of Theorem
15
.

6.2.2.
The Span Fusion Operation

The
span-fusion

\spanfusion
is a binary
operation
\spans\times\spans\to\spans
defined by
[i,j\rangle\spanfusion[i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\rangle=[\min\{i,i^{\prime}\},\max\{j,j^{\prime}\}\rangle
and

[i,j\rangle\spanfusion\undefin=\undefin\spanfusion[i,j\rangle=[i,j\rangle
.
Intuitively speaking, the operation
\spanfusion

constructs the set-union of two spans and fills in the gaps to turn it
into a valid span.
Note that
\spanfusion
is obviously associative.
For a set
K\subseteq\spans(w)
, we define

\bigspanfusion(K)=\undefin
if
K=\emptyset
and

\bigspanfusion(K)=\bigspanfusion(K\setminus\{s\})\spanfusion s
if

s\in K
.

We next lift this operation to an operation on spanners with the following intended meaning. In a table
S(w)
for some spanner
S
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, and
w\in\Sigma^{*}
, we want to replace a specified set of columns
\{\mathsf{y}_{1},\mathsf{y}_{2},\ldots,\mathsf{y}_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{X}
by a single new column
\mathsf{x}
that, for each row
t
(i. e., span-tuple
t
) in
S(w)
, contains the span
\bigspanfusion(\{t(\mathsf{y}_{i})\mid i\in[k]\})
.

{defi}

Let
\lambda\subseteq\mathcal{X}
and let
\mathsf{x}
be a new variable
with
\mathsf{x}\notin\mathcal{X}\setminus\lambda
. For any

\mathcal{X}
-tuple
t
,
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(t)
is the

((\mathcal{X}\setminus\lambda)\cup\{\mathsf{x}\})
-tuple with

(\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(t))(\mathsf{x})=\bigspanfusion(\{t(\mathsf{y})\mid\mathsf{y}\in\lambda\})
and

(\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(t))(\mathsf{z})=t(\mathsf{z})
for
every
\mathsf{z}\in\mathcal{X}\setminus\lambda
. For a set
R
of

\mathcal{X}
-tuples,
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(R)=\{\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(t)\mid t\in R\}
. Moreover,
for a spanner
S
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, the spanner

\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(S)
over
\Sigma
and
((\mathcal{X}\setminus\lambda)\cup\{\mathsf{x}\})
is defined by
(\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(S))(w)=\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}(S(w))
for every word
w
.

We use the following generalised application of the operation
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}
. For
\Lambda=\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\allowbreak\lambda_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
such that all
\lambda_{i}
with
i\in[k]
are pairwise disjoint, a spanner
S
over
\mathcal{X}
and fresh variables
\mathsf{x}_{1},\mathsf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathsf{x}_{k}
, we define
\bigspanfusion_{\{\lambda_{i}\to\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid i\in[k]\}}(S)=\bigspanfusion_{\lambda_{1}\to\mathsf{x}_{1}}(\bigspanfusion_{\lambda_{2}\to\mathsf{x}_{2}}(\ldots\bigspanfusion_{\lambda_{k}\to\mathsf{x}_{k}}(S)\ldots))
. If the new variables
\mathsf{x}_{i}
are clear from the context, we also write
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda}
or
\bigspanfusion_{\{\lambda_{i}\mid i\in[k]\}}
instead of
\bigspanfusion_{\lambda\to\mathsf{x}}
or
\bigspanfusion_{\{\lambda_{i}\to\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid i\in[k]\}}
, respectively.
