be a subword-marked language over
\{\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b}\}
and
\{\mathsf{y}_{1},\mathsf{y}_{2},\mathsf{y}_{3},\mathsf{y}_{4}\}
, and let
\Lambda=\{\{\mathsf{y}_{1},\mathsf{y}_{2}\}\to\mathsf{x}_{1},\{\mathsf{y}_{3},\mathsf{y}_{4}\}\to\mathsf{x}_{2}\}
. Then

\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket(w)=\{\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}([1,3\rangle,[3,4\rangle,[3,4\rangle,[4,7\rangle)\}=\{([1,4\rangle,[3,7\rangle)\}=\llbracket L\rrbracket(w)

In fact, it can be easily verified that
\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\llbracket L\rrbracket
.

6.2.3.
The Split Operation

Intuitively speaking, a split
t^{\prime}
of a span-tuple
t
is any
span-tuple obtained from
t
by splitting each span
t(\mathsf{x})
into
several spans, e. g., splitting
[3,24\rangle
into spans

[3,5\rangle,[5,17\rangle,[17,17\rangle,[17,24\rangle
. Any
such split
t^{\prime}
can be easily translated back into
t
by applications
of the span fusion, i. e.,
\bigspanfusion_{\{\lambda_{\mathsf{x}}\to\mathsf{x}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}}(t^{\prime})=t
, where the sets

\lambda_{\mathsf{x}}
are the variables used for the split version of

t(\mathsf{x})
. There are two important aspects of this
operation. Firstly, if we allow large enough splits, i. e., if we
choose the sets
\lambda_{\mathsf{x}}
large enough, then we can always
split in such a way that all variables are non-overlapping. Secondly,
the split of a regular spanner (i. e., the spanner that extracts all splits of the original span-tuples) is also a regular spanner. Let us next define this formally.

Let us first recall the definition of non-overlapping variables, which
has already been introduced
in Section
2
. Let
L
be a subword-marked
language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, let
w\in L
and
t=\mathsf{st}(w)
. We say that variables
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{X}

are
non-overlapping
(
with respect to
w
(
or

t
)) if
t(\mathsf{x})=t(\mathsf{y})
or
t(\mathsf{x})
and
t(\mathsf{y})
are
disjoint (i. e.,
t(\mathsf{x})=[\ell_{\mathsf{x}},r_{\mathsf{x}}\rangle
and

t(\mathsf{y})=[\ell_{\mathsf{y}},r_{\mathsf{y}}\rangle
with
r_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant\ell_{\mathsf{y}}
or
r_{\mathsf{y}}\leqslant\ell_{\mathsf{x}}
). The variables

\mathsf{x}
and
\mathsf{y}
are non-overlapping with respect to the
subword-marked language
L
, if
\mathsf{x}
and
\mathsf{y}
are
non-overlapping with respect to every
w\in L
.

For any set
\mathcal{X}
of variables, we define the
extended variable set

\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
for
\mathcal{X}
by
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X}):=\bigcup_{\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\mathsf{x}^{2},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{\varno}\}
, where
\varno:=4|\mathcal{X}|^{2}-1
(the choice of the number
\varno
is crucial and will become clear later). Intuitively, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, the extended variable set for
\mathcal{X}
contains
\varno
new variables, e. g.,
\textsf{ext}(\{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y},\mathsf{z}\})=\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{37},\mathsf{y}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{y}^{37},\mathsf{z}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{z}^{37}\}
. With respect to
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
, we can also make the following observation.

{obs}

For every set
\mathcal{X}
of variables, we have that
|\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})|=\bigO(|\mathcal{X}|^{3})
.

Let
t
be an
\mathcal{X}
-tuple. Any
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
-tuple
t^{\prime}
is called a
split
of
t
if it satisfies the following properties:

•

For every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
,

–

if
t(\mathsf{x})=\undefin
, then
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})=t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{2})=\ldots=t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{\varno})=\undefin
,

–

if
t(\mathsf{x})=[k,\ell\rangle
, then, for every
i\in[\varno]
,
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{i})=[k_{i},\ell_{i}\rangle
such that
k_{1}=k
,
\ell_{\varno}=\ell
, and, for every
i\in[\varno-1]
,
\ell_{i}=k_{i+1}
.

•

Any two variables of
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
are non-overlapping with respect to
t
.

For example, let
t
be an
\{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\}
-tuple with
t(\mathsf{x})=[3,24\rangle
and
t(\mathsf{y})=[7,15\rangle
. Then a possible
split of
t
would be the
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
-tuple
t^{\prime}
with

t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})=[3,7\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{2})=[7,12\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{3})=[12,15\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{4})=[15,24\rangle
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{j})=[24,24\rangle
for
every
j\in\{5,6,\ldots,17\}
, and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{1})=[7,12\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{2})=[12,12\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{3})=[12,15\rangle
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{j})=[15,15\rangle
for every
j\in\{4,5\ldots,17\}
.

For every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, we define
\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}=\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\mathsf{x}^{2},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{\varno}\}
. Hence,
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})=\bigcup_{\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}
. By definition, every split
t^{\prime}
of
t
satisfies
\bigspanfusion_{\{\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}\to\mathsf{x}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}}(t^{\prime})=t
.

We can define splits analogously for subword-marked words. Let
L
be a subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
. For any
w\in L
, we say that a subword-marked word
w^{\prime}
over
\Sigma
and
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
is a
split
of
w
, if
\mathfrak{e}(w)=\mathfrak{e}(w^{\prime})
and
\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})
is a split of
\mathsf{st}(w)
.

For an
\mathcal{X}
-tuple
t
(or subword-marked word
w
), let
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(t)
(
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(w)
, respectively) be the set of all splits of
t
(splits of
w
, respectively).
For any subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, let
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)=\{\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(w)\mid w\in L\}
, and let
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)=\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket
.

We will next see that the split of any regular spanner is also a
regular spanner. We will show that any
\NFA

M
for a
subword-marked language
L
can be modified such that it accepts
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)
. To this end, we simply non-deterministically use the markers

Step 1
(Changing
M
into
M^{\prime}
): The
\NFA

M^{\prime}
simulates the computation of
M
on
w
, but with the following differences. Whenever
M
opens some variable
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, then
M^{\prime}
opens variable
\mathsf{x}^{1}
. At any point in the computation,
M^{\prime}
can nondeterministically choose some currently open variable
\mathsf{x}^{j}
with
j<\varno
, and then close
\mathsf{x}^{j}
and open
\mathsf{x}^{j+1}
(observe that closing
\mathsf{x}^{\varno}
is not included here). Whenever
M
closes some variable
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, then
M^{\prime}
closes the currently open variable
\mathsf{x}^{j}
(which may be
\mathsf{x}^{\varno}
) and then opens and closes all remaining variables
\mathsf{x}^{j+1},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{\varno}
.

Let us say that a subword-marked word
w^{\prime}
over
\Sigma
and
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
is a
pseudo-split
of a subword marked word
w
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, if the first property of the definition of splits is satisfied:

•

if
\mathsf{st}(w)(\mathsf{x})=\undefin
, then
\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})(\mathsf{x}^{1})=\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})(\mathsf{x}^{2})=\ldots=\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})(\mathsf{x}^{\varno})=\undefin
,

•

if
\mathsf{st}(w)(\mathsf{x})=[k,\ell\rangle
, then, for every
i\in[\varno]
,
\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})(\mathsf{x}^{i})=[k_{i},\ell_{i}\rangle
such that
k_{1}=k
,
\ell_{\varno}=\ell
, and, for every
i\in[\varno-1]
,
\ell_{i}=k_{i+1}
.

It can be easily seen that
M^{\prime}
accepts exactly all subword-marked words over
\Sigma
and
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
that are pseudo-splits of subword-marked words accepted by
M
.

We now have to filter out those pseudo-splits which are not valid splits, i. e., those that do not satisfy the second property of the definition of splits: any two variables of
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
are non-overlapping with respect to
\mathsf{st}(w^{\prime})
.

Step 2
(Changing
M^{\prime}
into
M^{\prime\prime}
): The
\NFA

M^{\prime\prime}
simulates the computation of
M^{\prime}
on
w
, but it can interrupt certain computations and reject the input as follows. Let us assume that
M^{\prime}
reads a symbol
\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal{X}}
, which, since
\Gamma
is non-empty, means that some variable is either opened or closed at this step. Then
M^{\prime}
checks whether there is some variable
\mathsf{y}
that is open right before
M^{\prime}
reads
\Gamma
and
\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-8.18211pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\kern-7.68211pt{}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-8.18211pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 8.071pt{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\kern-7.68211pt{}\kern 8.071pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-5.74321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 5.6321pt{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\kern-5.24321pt{}\kern 5.6321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\triangleleft^{{\kern-4.65433pt\mathchoice{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.0pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 4.54321pt{\mathsf{y}}}}_{{\kern-4.15433pt{}\kern 4.54321pt\mathchoice{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.22778pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.25945pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.61389pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\notin\Gamma
and, if this is the case,
M^{\prime}
interrupts the computation and rejects.

Obviously, if some
w^{\prime}\in\lang(M^{\prime})
is a valid split of some
w\in\lang(M)
, then upon reading
w^{\prime}
the situation that causes
M^{\prime\prime}
to interrupt will never occur, which means that
w^{\prime}\in\lang(M^{\prime\prime})
. On the other hand, if some
w^{\prime}\in\lang(M^{\prime})
is only a pseudo-split of some
w\in\lang(M)
, but not a valid split, then there are two variables in
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
that are overlapping with respect to
w^{\prime}
, which means that any computation of
M^{\prime\prime}
on
w^{\prime}
must lead to the situation that causes
M^{\prime}
to interrupt and reject. Consequently,
M^{\prime\prime}
accepts the subset of
\lang(M^{\prime})
of valid splits. Thus,
\lang(M^{\prime\prime})=\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)

Let
L
be a regular subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, and let
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
be a string-equality selection with
E=\{\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
. The next question is how we can represent the spanner
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
by first applying the split version of
\llbracket L\rrbracket
, then applying some string-equality selections tailored to the split span relation, and then, finally, using the span-fusion operation to translate back the split span-tuples into the original span-tuples. More precisely, we want to represent
\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)
in the form
(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))
, for some suitable string-equality selection
\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}
.

Intuitively speaking,
\varsigma_{E^{\prime}}^{=}
simulates
\varsigma^{=}_{E}
in the sense that for any
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
it checks the string-equality of
t(\mathsf{x})
and
t(\mathsf{y})
by checking the string-equalities for all the variable pairs
t(\mathsf{x}_{j})
and
t(\mathsf{y}_{j})
for every
j\in[\varno]
.
More formally, for every
i\in[k]
and every
j\in[\varno]
, we define
\mathcal{Y}_{i}^{j}=\{\mathsf{x}^{j}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}\}
,
and we set
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})=\varsigma_{\{\mathcal{Y}_{i}^{j}\mid j\in[\varno],i\in[k]\}}^{=}
.

The following lemma follows more or less directly from the
definitions. Recall that, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, we have defined
\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}=\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\mathsf{x}^{2},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{\varno}\}
.

Lemma 17
.

Let
L
be a regular subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, let
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
be a string-equality selection with
E\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
, let
\Lambda=\{\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}\to\mathsf{x}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}
and let
w\in\Sigma^{*}
. Then
(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))(w)\subseteq(\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket))(w)
.

Proof 6.4
.

Let
t\in(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))(w)
. This means that there is a
split
t^{\prime}
of
t
with
t^{\prime}\in(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)))(w)
and
\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(t^{\prime})=t
. Due to the string-equality selection
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})
,
this means that, for every
i\in[k]
and all
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
, if
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})\neq\undefin
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{1})\neq\undefin
, then the spans
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{j})
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{j})
refer to equal factors of
w
for every
j\in[\varno]
. This directly
implies that also
(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(t^{\prime}))(\mathsf{x})
and

(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(t^{\prime}))(\mathsf{y})
refer to equal factors in
w
,
which means that
\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(t^{\prime})\in(\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket))(w)
. Since

\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(t^{\prime})=t
, this means that
t\in(\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket))(w)
.

The converse of Lemma
17
does not
necessarily hold. This is due to the fact that for a
t\in(\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket))(w)
and
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
such that
t(\mathsf{x})
and
t(\mathsf{y})
refer to equal factors, there might not be any split
t^{\prime}
of
t
with the property that, for every
j\in[\varno]
,
t(\mathsf{x}^{j})
and
t(\mathsf{y}^{j})
refer to equal factors, which is necessary for
t
being in
(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))(w)
. Let us clarify this with an example.

be a regular subword-marked language over
\Sigma=\{\mathtt{a}\}
and
\mathcal{X}=\{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\}
. Then
t=([1,19\rangle,[2,20\rangle)
is in
(\varsigma_{\{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\}}^{=}\llbracket L\rrbracket)(\mathtt{a}^{19})
. Now consider an arbitrary split
t^{\prime}
of
t
. By definition,
t^{\prime}
is a span-tuple over
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})=\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{17},\mathsf{y}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{y}^{17}\}
, such that

•

t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})=[1,\ell_{1}\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{2})=[\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{3})=[\ell_{2},\ell_{3}\rangle,\ldots,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{17})=[\ell_{16},19\rangle
,

•

t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{1})=[2,k_{1}\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{2})=[k_{1},k_{2}\rangle,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{3})=[k_{2},k_{3}\rangle,\ldots,t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{17})=[k_{16},20\rangle
,

•

any two variables from
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
are non-overlapping.

Now assume that
t^{\prime}
also has the property that, for every
i\in[17]
,
t(\mathsf{x}^{i})
and
t(\mathsf{y}^{i})
refer to equal factors of
\mathtt{a}^{19}
. For simplicity, let us assume that none of the spans are
empty (we will briefly discuss the general case below). Since
\mathsf{x}^{1}
and
\mathsf{y}^{1}
are non-overlapping, we must have
\ell_{1}=2
, which means that
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})
refers to a factor
\mathtt{a}
. Since, by assumption,
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{y}^{1})
refer to equal factors, we therefore must also have
k_{1}=3
. Analogously, we can conclude that
\ell_{2}=3
and
k_{2}=4
, and
inductively repeating this argument implies that every span must refer
to a factor of size

, which is not possible since
t(\mathsf{x})
and

t(\mathsf{y})
both refer to a factor of size
18
, and we only have
17

variables
\mathsf{x}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{17}
and
17
variables

\mathsf{y}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{y}^{17}
. Note that the same kind of
pigeon-hole argument also applies if some of the spans of the
variables from
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
are empty.
Consequently, no split
t^{\prime}
can have
the property that, for every
i\in[17]
,
t(\mathsf{x}^{i})
and

t(\mathsf{y}^{i})
refer to equal factors of
\mathtt{a}^{19}
, which means that

t
cannot be in

(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))(\mathtt{a}^{19})
.

Note that this problem cannot be resolved by simply enlarging the
extended variable set
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
to
\{\mathsf{x}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{x}^{p},\mathsf{y}^{1},\ldots,\mathsf{y}^{p}\}
for some sufficiently large

p
, since then the same contradiction can be obtained with the
document
\mathtt{a}^{p+2}
.

This example points out that using a string-equality selection with respect to variables that can overlap is the reason that the converse of Lemma
17
is not necessarily true. We will next restrict the string-equality selections accordingly.

Let
L
be a regular subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
, and let
E=
\{\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
. We say that
E
is
non-overlapping
(
with respect to
L
) if all
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\bigcup_{i\in[k]}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
are non-overlapping with respect to
L
.

Lemma 18
.

Let
L
be a regular subword-marked language over
\Sigma
and

\mathcal{X}
, let
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
be a string-equality selection such
that
E\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
is non-overlapping with
respect to
L
, let
\Lambda=\{\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}\to\mathsf{x}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}
and let
w\in\Sigma^{*}
. Then

(\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket))(w)\subseteq(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))(w)
.

Proof 6.5
.

Let
E=\{\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathcal{Z}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{k}\}
, and
let
t\in(\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket))(w)
. We will
show that there is a split
t^{\prime}
of
t
, such that
t^{\prime}\in(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket))(w)
. If such a split exists, then,
due to the fact that
\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(t^{\prime})=t
, we have
t\in(\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)))(w)
.

Since
E
is a non-overlapping string equality selection, we know that all the spans
t(\mathsf{x})
with
\mathsf{x}\in\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
are pairwise non-overlapping. However, it is not sufficient to simply create the span-tuple
t^{\prime}
where, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
,
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})=t(\mathsf{x})=[\ell,k\rangle
and
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{i})=[k,k\rangle
for every
i\in\{2,3,\ldots,\varno\}
. In general, this definition would yield a span-tuple
t^{\prime}
that is not a valid split of
t
, since
t
may have overlapping spans with respect to variables that are not in
\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\mathcal{Z}_{i}
, i. e., for a variable
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\setminus(\bigcup^{k}_{i=1}\mathcal{Z}_{i})
and some other variable
\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{X}
, the spans
t(\mathsf{x})
and
t(\mathsf{y})
can be overlapping.

For every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
with
t(\mathsf{x})\neq\undefin
, let
t(\mathsf{x})=[\ell_{\mathsf{x}},k_{\mathsf{x}}\rangle
. We observe that every
t(\mathsf{x})
can be interpreted as the interval
\{\ell_{\mathsf{x}},\ell_{\mathsf{x}}+1,\ldots,k_{\mathsf{x}}\}
.
A
split point of
t(\mathsf{x})
is any element from
\{\ell_{\mathsf{x}},\ell_{\mathsf{x}}+1,\ldots,k_{\mathsf{x}}\}
. Now let us assume that, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, we have a set
\{p_{\mathsf{x},1},p_{\mathsf{x},2},\ldots,p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}\}
of split points of
t(\mathsf{x})
, which satisfy the following properties.

(1)

For every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
,
p_{\mathsf{x},1}=\ell_{\mathsf{x}}
,
p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}=k_{\mathsf{x}}
and
s_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant\varno+1
.

(2)

For every
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{X}
and every
i_{\mathsf{x}}\in[s_{\mathsf{x}}-1]
and
i_{\mathsf{y}}\in[s_{\mathsf{y}}-1]
, the spans
[p_{\mathsf{x},i_{\mathsf{x}}},p_{\mathsf{x},i_{\mathsf{x}}+1}\rangle
and
[p_{\mathsf{y},i_{\mathsf{y}}},p_{\mathsf{y},i_{\mathsf{y}}+1}\rangle
are non-overlapping.

(3)

For every
i\in[k]
and
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
,
s_{\mathsf{x}}=s_{\mathsf{y}}
and, for every
j\in[s_{\mathsf{x}}]
,
p_{\mathsf{x},j}-\ell_{\mathsf{x}}=p_{\mathsf{y},j}-\ell_{\mathsf{y}}
.

It can be easily seen that such split points induce a split
t^{\prime}
of
t
such that
t^{\prime}\in(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket))(w)
. Indeed, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, we define
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{1})=[p_{\mathsf{x},1},p_{\mathsf{x},2}\rangle
,
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{2})=[p_{\mathsf{x},2},p_{\mathsf{x},3}\rangle
,
\ldots
,
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{s_{\mathsf{x}}-1})=[p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}-1},p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}\rangle
, and we define
t^{\prime}(\mathsf{x}^{q})=[p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}},p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}\rangle
for every
q
with
s_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant q\leqslant\varno
. Since
s_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant\varno+1
for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, this is well-defined. Due to the first property of the split points, the span-tuple
t^{\prime}
satisfies the first condition of a split, and due to the second property of the split points, it also satisfies the second condition of a split. Thus,
t^{\prime}
is a split of
t
. Since
t
satisfies the string-equality selection
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
, we must have
k_{\mathsf{x}}-\ell_{\mathsf{x}}=k_{\mathsf{y}}-\ell_{\mathsf{y}}
for every
\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}
and
i\in[k]
. The fact that
t
satisfies the string equality selection
\varsigma_{E}^{=}
together with the third property of the split points directly implies that
t^{\prime}
satisfies the string-equality selection
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})
. This means that
t^{\prime}\in(\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket))(w)
.

In order to complete the proof, we have to show that split points with the above properties can be created. Let us first observe that if we declare some elements of
\{1,2,\ldots,|w|+1\}
to be
general split points
, then this defines a set
\{p_{\mathsf{x},1},p_{\mathsf{x},2},\ldots,p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}\}
of split points for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
. More precisely, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
,
\{p_{\mathsf{x},1},p_{\mathsf{x},2},\ldots,p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}\}
is exactly the set of all general split points
p
that satisfy
p\in\{\ell_{\mathsf{x}},\ell_{\mathsf{x}}+1,\ldots,k_{\mathsf{x}}\}
. We declare the general split points in two steps.

•

First step
: For every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
with
t(\mathsf{x})\neq\undefin
, both
\ell_{\mathsf{x}}
and
r_{\mathsf{x}}
are declared general split points.

•

Second step
: Let us call the general split points added in the first step
old
general split points, and the ones to be added in this step
new
general split points. For every
i\in[k]
we now proceed as follows.

Let
\mathcal{Z}_{i}=\{\mathsf{z}_{1},\mathsf{z}_{2},\ldots,\mathsf{z}_{k_{i}}\}
. For every
j\in[k_{i}]
, let
\{q_{j,1},q_{j,2},\ldots,q_{j,s_{j}}\}
be the old general split points in the interval
\{\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}},\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}+1,\ldots,k_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}\}
, i. e., the old general split points defined in the first step that will be split points of
t(\mathsf{z}_{j})
, and let
A_{j}=\{q_{j,1}-\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}},q_{j,2}-\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}},\ldots,q_{j,s_{j}}-\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}\}
be the set of these split points shifted to the left by
\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}
. Then, we join all these sets into
B_{i}=\bigcup^{k_{i}}_{j=1}A_{j}
and shift all these points back to their corresponding positions in each of the intervals
\{\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}},\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}+1,\ldots,k_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}\}
, i. e., we declare all elements of
\{p+\ell_{\mathsf{z}_{j}}\mid j\in[k_{i}],p\in B_{i}\}
to be new split points.

This concludes the definition of general split points and therefore defines, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
, a set
\{p_{\mathsf{x},1},p_{\mathsf{x},2},\ldots,p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}\}
of split points of
t(\mathsf{x})
. By definition, for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
,
p_{\mathsf{x},1}=\ell_{\mathsf{x}}
and
p_{\mathsf{x},s_{\mathsf{x}}}=k_{\mathsf{x}}
, since both
\ell_{\mathsf{x}}
and
k_{\mathsf{x}}
are declared general split points in the first step.

We now estimate the total number of general split points introduced by the two steps from above. We first note that in the first step we have introduced at most
2|\mathcal{X}|
general split points (the maximum
2|\mathcal{X}|
is reached if
t(\mathsf{x})\neq\undefin
for all variables
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
). In the second step, for every
i\in[k]
, we create at most
k_{i}|B_{i}|
new general split points, where
B_{i}=\bigcup^{k_{i}}_{j=1}A_{j}
. Since each
A_{j}
only contains old general split points, we know that
|A_{j}|\leqslant 2|\mathcal{X}|
for every
j\in[k_{i}]
. Thus,
|B_{i}|\leqslant k_{i}2|\mathcal{X}|
. This means that in the second step, we create at most
\sum^{k}_{i=1}k_{i}2|\mathcal{X}|=2|\mathcal{X}|\sum^{k}_{i=1}k_{i}\leqslant 2|\mathcal{X}|^{2}
. Finally, we conclude that the total number of general split points is at most
2|\mathcal{X}|+2|\mathcal{X}|^{2}\leqslant 4|\mathcal{X}|^{2}
. In particular, this means that
s_{\mathsf{x}}\leqslant 4|\mathcal{X}|^{2}=\varno+1
for every
\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}
. We therefore conclude that the defined split points satisfy the first property mentioned above.

That the split points satisfy the second and third property mentioned above is obvious by construction.

6.2.4.
Core-Spanners with Non-Overlapping String-Equality Selections

We can now plug together the previously proven lemmas in the way sketched at the beginning of Section
6
in order to obtain this section’s main result. In particular, note that due to the normal form of Lemma
1
, every core spanner (with non-overlapping string equality selections) has a representation as in the statement of the following theorem.

Theorem 19
.

Let
S
be a core spanner with
S=\pi_{\mathcal{Y}}\varsigma_{E}^{=}(S^{\prime})
, where
S^{\prime}
is a regular
spanner over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}
,
\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{X}

and
E\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})
such that
E
is
non-overlapping with respect to
S^{\prime}
. There
are a variable set
\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
,
a reference-bounded refl-spanner
S^{\prime\prime}
over
\Sigma
and
\mathcal{X}^{\prime}
, and a set
\Lambda\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime})
such that
S=\pi_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(S^{\prime\prime})
. Moreover,
|\mathcal{X}^{\prime}|=\bigO(|\mathcal{X}|^{3})
.

Proof 6.6
.

Let
L
be a regular subword-marked language with
S^{\prime}=\llbracket L\rrbracket
. Since
E
is non-overlapping with respect to
L
,
Lemmas
17
and
18

imply that

\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)\ \ =\ \ \bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket),

where

\Lambda=\{\lambda^{\varno}_{\mathsf{x}}\to\mathsf{x}\mid\mathsf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}
.

Moreover,
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)
is a subword-marked language over

\Sigma
and
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
such that any two variables from
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
are
non-overlapping with respect to
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)
. This directly
implies that every variable from
\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
is simple with
respect to
\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)
. By applying
Theorem
15
, we can conclude that
there is a reference-bounded regular ref-language
L^{\prime}
over
\Sigma
and

\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})
with
\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket=\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)
. Hence,
S=\pi_{\mathcal{Y}}\varsigma_{E}^{=}(\llbracket L\rrbracket)=\pi_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(\varsigma_{E}^{=})(\llbracket\textsf{split}_{\mathcal{X}}(L)\rrbracket)=\pi_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigspanfusion_{\Lambda}(\llbracket L^{\prime}\rrbracket)
.

Finally, by Observation
6.2.3
, we have that
|\textsf{ext}(\mathcal{X})|=\bigO(|\mathcal{X}|^{3})
.

7.
Conclusion

In this work, we introduced reference-bounded refl-spanners, a new fragment of core spanners. In terms of expressive power, this fragment
is slightly less powerful than
the class of core spanners, but has lower evaluation complexity (see
Table
1
, and note further that these upper bounds even hold for refl-spanners that are
not
necessarily reference-bounded). If we add the
span-fusion
– a natural binary operation on spanners – followed by a projection,
to reference-bounded
refl-spanners (see
Section
6
)
then they
have the same expressive power as
core spanners with
non-overlapping
string-equality
selections. This demonstrates that our formalism covers all aspects of
core spanners except for the possibility of applying string-equality
selections on variables with overlapping spans. Moreover, since we
achieve better complexities for refl-spanners compared to core
spanners, this also shows that overlapping string-equality selections, followed by a projection, are a source of complexity for core spanners.

From a conceptional point of view, our new angle was to treat the classical two-stage approach of core spanners, i. e., first producing the output table of a regular spanner and then filtering it by applying the string-equality selections, as a single
\NFA
. This is achieved by using ref-words in order to represent a document along with a span-tuple
that satisfies the string-equality selections
, instead of just using subword-marked words to represent a document along with a span-tuple, which might not satisfy the string-equality selections and therefore will be filtered out later in the second evaluation stage.

A question that is left open for further research is about enumeration for some
fragment of core spanners
strictly more powerful than the regular spanners. In this regard, we note
that for efficient enumeration for (some fragments of)
core spanners,
we must overcome the general intractability of
\NonemptProb
(which we have for core spanners as well as for (reference bounded) refl-spanners).
We believe that refl-spanners are a promising candidate for further
restrictions that may lead to a fragment of
core spanners
that enables constant delay enumeration.
